title: Checkpoint: Bets and Expected Value
objective: After this level you can judge a bet or an everyday gamble by its odds and its expected value.
summary: Judge any bet by three questions: what is the chance, what is it worth on average (expected value), and how bad can it get. When the math is slippery, count cases or simulate.

cards.headline: A roulette spin, a lottery ticket, a parking meter: one checklist fits them all.
cards.body: Chapter 4 handed you the tools one level at a time. This checkpoint lines them up into three questions you can ask of any bet.

cards.headline: Three questions for any bet
cards.body: First: what's the chance? Turn the odds into a probability by adding the two numbers: 3 to 1 against is 1 in 4. Second: what's it worth on average? Multiply each outcome by its chance and add: that's the expected value. Third: how bad can it get? A win-or-lose $1,000 coin flip averages $0, just like a $1 flip, and risk-averse people rightly prefer the sure thing.

items.label: Powerball
points: About half of each dollar goes to prizes

items.label: Insurance
points: Premiums cover claims, costs and profit
Buyers lose a little to avoid a big loss

cards.headline: When the math gets slippery, count
cards.body: Some chances fool almost everyone. In the Monty Hall puzzle, switching wins 2 times in 3, even though two doors are left. When your gut and the math disagree, count the cases one by one, or do what Ulam did: run lots of pretend trials and count how often you win.

cards.headline: Chapter 4 complete
learned: How to judge any bet by its chance, its expected value and how bad it can get.
Why the casino and the lottery win on average, and how to turn odds into a probability.
Why insurance loses money on average yet can still be a sensible choice.
How switching doors wins 2 times in 3, and how simulations estimate chances too hard to work out.

questions.prompt: Which three questions should you ask of any bet?

options.label: How big is the prize, how cheap is it, how many people play?
options.rationale: Prize and price alone skip the chance and the risk.

options.label: Is it on a streak, is it lucky, is it due?
options.rationale: Streaks and luck do not change the chances.

options.label: What's the chance, what's the average, how bad can it get?
Who runs it, who wins, who pays?
options.rationale: None of these measure the bet itself.

questions.explanation: Chance (from the odds), expected value (the average), and the worst case (the spread).

questions.prompt: A prize is offered at odds of 7 to 1 against, so the chance of winning it is _____.

options.label: 1 in 6
options.rationale: Add the two numbers; don't subtract.

questions.explanation: 7 ways to lose plus 1 way to win makes 8, so the chance is 1 in 8.

questions.prompt: American roulette pays 35 to 1 on a single number. Why does that give the casino an edge?

options.label: The true odds against one number are 37 to 1
Roulette wheels are weighted toward green
options.rationale: Every pocket is one of 38; the payout is short.

options.label: The casino keeps your stake when you win
The true odds are 35 to 1, so the edge comes from tips
options.rationale: With 38 pockets the true odds are 37 to 1.

questions.explanation: With 1 winning pocket and 37 losing ones, a fair payout would be 37 to 1; paying 35 leaves the casino 2 parts in 38.

questions.prompt: Match each bet with its key fact.

pairs.right: Premiums cover claims, costs and profit

questions.explanation: American roulette has a house edge of about 5.26%, Powerball's jackpot odds are 1 in 292,201,338, and insurance premiums cover claims, costs and profit.

questions.prompt: Insurance and a win-or-lose $1,000 coin flip teach one shared lesson. Which is it?

options.label: A negative expected value is always a mistake
options.rationale: Insurance has one and can still be sensible.

options.label: The average alone does not show how bad things can get
Bigger stakes always mean a bigger average
Only lotteries have long odds
options.rationale: The shared point is about spread, not about how long the odds are.

questions.explanation: Both show that expected value hides the spread: judge a gamble by its average and its worst case.
